hazard_level: Low to Moderate (High if electrolytic capacitors leak or legacy units contain PCBs)
hazards: Stored residual high-voltage electrical charge in large power-supply capacitors
Corrosive chemical electrolytes inside aluminum electrolytic capacitors
Lead in older solder terminations and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in pre-1980s industrial capacitors
safe_handling: Safely discharge large capacitors with a bleed resistor before handling
Handle loose or leaking capacitors using insulated tweezers or nitrile gloves
Store in dry, rigid, non-conductive containers away from heat sources
unsafe_actions: Never puncture, crush, or incinerate capacitors (high risk of bursting or explosion)
Never touch bare leads of large charged capacitors directly
Do not throw loose capacitors into regular dustbins or wash leaking fluid down drains
what_to_do_if_damaged: If a capacitor is bulging, vented, or leaking electrolyte, avoid bare-skin contact. Wear nitrile gloves, wipe any residue with a disposable absorbent cloth, and seal both the capacitor and cloth in a labeled hazardous e-waste pouch.
disposal_route: Segregate and hand over to a CPCB-authorized e-waste dismantler or hazardous electronic waste treatment facility (TSDF); legacy PCB-containing capacitors require specialized hazardous waste incineration.
recoverable_materials: Silver, palladium, and copper (SMD terminations and leads)
environmental_impact: Improper dumping or burning causes electrolytic chemicals, heavy metals, and toxic gases to leach into soil, groundwater, and air.
